title: Maximum Depth of Binary Tree
problemStatement: Given the root of a binary tree, return its maximum depth (the number of nodes along the longest path from the root down to the farthest leaf node).
constraints: The number of nodes is in [0, 10^4]
approachSteps: The depth of a tree is naturally defined in terms of the depth of its subtrees — a strong signal to think recursively.
Base case: an empty tree (null node) has depth 0.
Recursive case: a node's depth is 1 (for itself) plus the larger of its left and right subtree depths.
Recurse on both children, then combine with max() and add 1.

bruteForce.approach: Iterative BFS level-by-level, counting levels — also O(n), just a different valid strategy (not really a 'worse' brute force here, both are optimal).
bruteForce.spaceComplexity: O(n) worst case for the queue

optimalApproach: Recursive DFS: depth(node) = 1 + max(depth(node.left), depth(node.right)), with depth(null) = 0.
timeComplexity: O(n) — visits every node exactly once.
spaceComplexity: O(h) for the recursion call stack, where h is the tree's height — O(log n) for a balanced tree, O(n) worst case for a skewed one.
followUps: How would you compute this iteratively with an explicit stack (avoiding recursion) or with BFS level counting?
How would you find the MINIMUM depth to a leaf, and why is that not simply the same recursion with min()?

title: Validate Binary Search Tree
problemStatement: Given the root of a binary tree, determine if it is a valid binary search tree (BST): every node's value must be strictly greater than all values in its left subtree and strictly less than all values in its right subtree, recursively for every node.

examples.explanation: The root's right child 4 has a left child 3, which is less than the root's value 5 — violates BST property even though 3 < 4 locally.

constraints: The number of nodes is in [1, 10^4]
approachSteps: A common bug: checking only node.left.val < node.val < node.right.val locally — this misses violations deeper in the subtree (see the example). You need each node checked against a valid RANGE, not just its immediate parent.
Pass down a (low, high) bound as you recurse: the current node's value must strictly fall within that range.
When recursing left, the upper bound tightens to the current node's value (everything in the left subtree must be less than it); the lower bound is unchanged.
When recursing right, the lower bound tightens to the current node's value; the upper bound is unchanged.
An empty subtree is trivially valid (base case). If any node violates its range, the whole tree is invalid.

bruteForce.approach: In-order traversal into a list, then check the list is strictly increasing — also O(n), a valid alternative optimal approach.

optimalApproach: DFS carrying a valid (low, high) range for each node, tightened appropriately when recursing into left/right subtrees.
spaceComplexity: O(h) recursion stack, h = tree height.
followUps: Why does the in-order-traversal approach also work — what property of BSTs does it rely on?
How would you handle duplicate values if the definition were '<=' instead of strict '<'?

title: Serialize and Deserialize Binary Tree
problemStatement: Design an algorithm to serialize a binary tree to a single string, and deserialize that string back to the original tree structure (not necessarily the same object references, but structurally identical).

examples.output: A string like "1,2,#,#,3,4,#,#,5,#,#" that can be deserialized back to the same tree.

constraints: The number of nodes is in [0, 10^4]
approachSteps: A tree needs enough information encoded that you can reconstruct its exact shape — an in-order traversal alone isn't enough (many trees share the same in-order sequence), so you need to record structure explicitly, including where children are missing.
Use preorder traversal (root, then left, then right) and explicitly write a sentinel (e.g. '#') for null children — this makes the encoding structurally unambiguous.
Serialize: recursively visit root, append its value, then recurse left, then recurse right; append '#' whenever you'd recurse into a null.

Deserialize: since it's preorder, the FIRST token is always the root. Consume tokens from the front of the list: build the root from the first token, then recursively build the left subtree (consuming more tokens), then the right subtree.
Because preorder + explicit null markers fully determines the recursive structure, a single left-to-right pass through the tokens correctly rebuilds the tree with no ambiguity.

bruteForce.approach: Level-order (BFS) serialization with null markers is also valid and commonly used — not really a 'worse' approach, just a different valid encoding (arguably more intuitive, slightly more bookkeeping).

optimalApproach: Preorder DFS serialization with explicit null sentinels; deserialization consumes the token stream in the same preorder sequence to rebuild the tree recursively.
timeComplexity: O(n) for both serialize and deserialize — each node/null slot is visited once.
spaceComplexity: O(n) for the serialized string/token list, plus O(h) recursion stack.
followUps: How would you serialize using level-order (BFS) instead, and what changes in the deserialization logic?
How would this approach need to change for an N-ary tree instead of a binary tree?

title: Same Tree
problemStatement: Given the roots of two binary trees p and q, return true if they are structurally identical and the nodes have the same values (not just isomorphic — exact same shape and values).

examples.explanation: Same values present, but different shape (left child vs right child).

constraints: The number of nodes in both trees is in [0, 100]
approachSteps: Two trees are the same only if their roots match AND both their left subtrees match AND both their right subtrees match — a direct recursive definition.
Base case: if both nodes are null, they trivially match (empty matches empty).
Base case: if exactly one is null (the other isn't), they can't match — different shape.
Recursive case: check the current values are equal, then recurse into left-vs-left and right-vs-right, requiring both to be true.

bruteForce.approach: Serialize both trees (e.g. preorder traversal with explicit null markers) into strings, then compare the strings for equality.

optimalApproach: Direct recursive comparison of both trees simultaneously, checking value equality and recursing into corresponding left/right subtrees.
timeComplexity: O(min(n, m)) — recursion can exit early on the first mismatch; O(n) worst case when the trees are actually identical (or identical in size).
spaceComplexity: O(h) recursion stack, where h is the smaller tree's height — no extra string buffer needed, unlike the serialization approach.
followUps: How would 'Subtree of Another Tree' (is q a subtree ANYWHERE inside p, not necessarily starting at the root) build on this same helper function?
How would you adapt this to check if two trees are mirror images of each other (Symmetric Tree) instead of identical?
